By the time Mara reached the house, the sea had given back the path.

She stood at the gate with her father’s key in her palm. Beyond it, the windows held the last of the afternoon light, and somewhere inside, a clock was still keeping time. She had expected silence. She had prepared herself for dust, for broken glass, for the particular emptiness of a place that no longer belonged to anyone.

Nothing had changed. That was the strange part. The blue door, the crooked letterbox, the rosemary growing through the step. All of it had carried on without her. Even the brass number beside the door had kept its shine, although there was nobody left to polish it.

She turned the key. The door caught against the floorboards, just as it always had, and she lifted it a little with her shoulder. Her body remembered the house before the rest of her was ready. There was the narrow hall. There was the mark where her bicycle had fallen. There was the kitchen, with its view of a sea that looked almost gentle from this distance.

On the table stood a cup and a folded newspaper. Beside them lay an envelope with her name on it. The handwriting was her father’s, but the stamp was new. Mara set down her bag and listened. Somewhere upstairs, the clock struck five.

She could have left then. Later, she would think about that moment more than any other: the open door behind her, the clear path back to the village, the ordinary afternoon waiting outside. Instead, she pulled out a chair. She had come all this way with a question. For the first time in seven years, she thought the house might have an answer.
